context: Here is the general scheme for proving that a decision problem (the function returns either 0 or 1 depending on membership in a specified language) is not computed by an algebraic circuit of low depth. Take a subset L of Rn which will be the decision problem and restrict your view to [0, 2m ]n , n is to be thought as the number of inputs and m as the bitlength of the integers we work with. Often in problems we only consider n and take m to be polynomial in n, it makes sense as in the bit world we may in polynomial time, only work with at most polynomial bit length integers. If L is complex enough the hope is that there will a a lot of alternations inside the hypercube [0, 2m ]n between areas belonging to L and areas not belonging to L. For instance if n = 1 (which is the only case studied by theorem 2), L is complex if [0, 2m ] L is equal to the union of exponentially many disjoint T intervals (exponential in m)8 .
